newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr goes to ground before rate showdown.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr goes to ground before rate showdown.

text.p: The Australian dollar spent a holiday-hit Monday session building a base around US$0.7820 support ahead of what promised to be a market-shaking week.
It was a shade off Friday's late level after U.S. investment banks sold into last week's one cent rally, but found enough exporter and Japanese bids to keep it above the 78 cent level.

Sentiment continued to be underpinned by expectations Tuesday's monthly meeting of the Reserve Bank board would not result in a rate cut, a belief which had seen yield spreads widen in the A$'s favour. This view was reinforced somewhat by a whopping 16.7 percent jump in April ANZ job ads data.
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the local currency had dug in at US$0.7824/29 having paced out a US$0.7819/7833 range for the day compared to a US$0.7831/36 finish Friday.

Traders said volume had been meagre with the market thinned by a holiday in Japan, but various probes in each direction last week had already established US$0.7790 as a base and US$0.7860 as the ceiling. A breakout from here could well require definitive news on the possibility of a rate cut.
Today's, admittedly secondary jobs data, had favoured the predominant market view that an official easing was unlikely in the next month or so.

The ANZ jobs ads index, which measures the number of job advertisements in major papers, jumped 16.7 percent in April the biggest monthly gain since the series began in 1975. These figures tended to be ignored by the market but do have a good track record as a guide to jobs growth around six months ahead.

"Trend growth is accelerating and the data are consistent with the creation of 17,000 jobs per month -- enough to begin reducing the unemployment rate," said Anthony Thompson, an economist at HSBC Markets.
"With this leading indicator of employment gathering pace, the case against a further rate cut is strengthened," he said.

The flicker of recovery in the labour market was vital for the outlook on monetary policy since it had been the weakness of jobs growth in February and March that had stirred speculation of an easing.

Indeed, there has been talk the RBA would cut in a hurry if the employment data for April due Thursday showed no sign of the expected pick up. Median forecasts are for jobs to rise 35,000 in April after falls of 33,900 in March and 7,200 in February.
But estimates ranged to a 5,000 drop, a result which would surely set the money markets baying for a cut, so the market was not getting too excited by the NAZ ads data just yet.

The outlook was further confused by the fact RBA governor Ian Macfarlane gave his first testimony on the course of monetary policy -- the Australian equivalent of the Humphrey Hawkins testimony in the U.S. -- to a Parliamentary committee at 10.00 am on Thursday.
Analysts were unsure exactly what to expect from this new procedure but at minimum looked for a statement that present policy was either appropriate or under review.
On the crosses the dollar was a shade softer at 99.04/14 yen from 99.15/25 late Friday and at 60.8 in trade weighted terms from 60.9. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
